summary: Records the practices used for running IETF Hackathons, which encourage the community to collaborate on running code for existing and evolving Internet standards. The practices cover events with in-person and remote participation, with adaptations for online-only events. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A hackathon is a work party where people write programs together to try out new ideas. This is the how-to for organizing one.

subtitle: Practical guide to organizing collaborative code events

tldr.problem: The IETF community benefits from collaborative hands-on work on running code for Internet standards, but organizing hackathons at scale requires coordination across scheduling, funding, tools, and participation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents the practices and logistics that have worked for IETF Hackathons: timing them with IETF meetings, securing sponsorships, using collaborative tooling, managing projects, and facilitating both in-person and remote participation.
tldr.outcome: IETF Hackathons have grown to host hundreds of participants working on dozens of projects, proving that collaborative code development strengthens standard development and attracts newcomers.

today: RFC 9311 documents the established practices for running IETF Hackathons. The hackathons continue at each IETF meeting, with 19+ projects and hundreds of participants, and have proven successful as both a community activity and an onboarding mechanism for newcomers.

sections.title: What Are IETF Hackathons
sections.content:
IETF Hackathons are free, open collaborative events where the IETF community works together on running code related to Internet standards. Unlike competitive hackathons elsewhere, IETF Hackathons are inclusive and collaborative, not contests. Participants range from software developers (the primary audience) to subject-matter experts, academics, and long-time IETF contributors.

The Hackathons serve multiple purposes: they advance standards by bringing fast, iterative open-source development practices into the IETF; they introduce newcomers and early-career professionals to the community; and they strengthen human connections. Code written in a programming language often communicates more clearly than opinions expressed in meetings or emails. The exchange of ideas, networking, and trust-building among participants are as valuable as the code produced.
sections.plainLanguage: At a hackathon, teams collaborate to write programs that implement or test Internet standards. It is free, friendly, and open to anyone—beginners and experts alike.

sections.title: Timing and Event Structure
sections.content:
The first IETF Hackathon was held the weekend before IETF 92 to avoid meeting conflicts while remaining convenient for attendees. This weekend-before timing quickly became the standard. The Hackathon traditionally runs Saturday and Sunday for roughly 30 hours, with a typical agenda: setup and informal discussion Saturday morning, team formation by mid-morning, hacking throughout Saturday and Sunday, and project result presentations Sunday afternoon before the IETF Lounge and opening reception.

The tight schedule (closing at 22:00 Saturday and ending at 16:00 Sunday) balances intensive work with participant wellness and accommodates the IETF meeting schedule. Hackdemo Happy Hour, held Monday evening, provides additional time for in-depth sharing of project results. The Code Lounge continues collaboration during the main IETF meeting. For online-only meetings, the entire work week is used, with kickoff Monday and closing Friday, allowing globally distributed teams to work asynchronously.
sections.plainLanguage: Hackathons happen over a weekend before the IETF meeting starts. Teams hack all day Saturday and Sunday morning, then show off what they built on Sunday afternoon.

sections.title: Sponsorship, Costs, and Resources
sections.content:
Participation is always free, so hackathons require outside funding. Initial sponsorship models had companies sponsor for one year (covering three hackathons). Cisco sponsored the first year, Huawei the second. When no sponsor stepped forward for the third year, the IETF integrated hackathon costs into the meeting budget, with sponsorship now optional and at different levels.

In-person expenses include meeting space (typically used from Friday afternoon through Sunday and later repurposed as the IETF Lounge), food and beverages (coffee, lunch, dinner, snacks), T-shirts (typically about 380 shirts, mixed sizes, at roughly $10 each), and stickers. Remote participation requires cloud infrastructure (Meetecho for streaming, Webex for team meetings, Gather for virtual socializing, and HackNet for network access). Online-only hackathons significantly increase remote participation costs because facilities are needed for 7-12 days rather than 3-4 days.
sections.plainLanguage: Hackathons cost money for space, food, and T-shirts. Companies sponsor to help, and the IETF covers the rest so everyone can participate for free.

sections.title: Projects and Presentations
sections.content:
Project management centers on several elements: Project Pitches were initially 5-10 minute talks by project champions describing goals and approach. As the Hackathon grew, pitches were dropped in favor of advance information shared on the project wiki, allowing participants to self-select. Project Results Presentations are brief summaries of what each team accomplished, lessons learned, and feedback for working groups. These are optional but most teams participate. Total presentation time is limited to 2 hours to accommodate all teams.

Champions are encouraged to use presentation templates (provided in PPTX, HTML, and other formats in a GitHub repository) and to upload results presentations to GitHub for permanence and reference. Remote presenters can use Meetecho's screen-sharing or have the Hackathon Chair manage slides. This structure balances open participation with manageable event logistics.
sections.plainLanguage: Each team picks a project related to a standard. At the end, they show what they built in a 3–5 minute talk. Everything is saved on GitHub for others to see later.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Tools
sections.content:
The IETF Hackathon leverages existing IETF infrastructure and tools. The Datatracker hosts the Hackathon as a non-standards team with its own space for materials. The IETF website hosts a Hackathon page with information and links to past and future events. Registration is through the IETF meeting registration system, is free, and is required. A wiki page serves as the primary information source, with separate pages for project information, a "lost and found" for unattached participants seeking teams, results presentation schedule, and in-person/online-only pages.

An email list handles announcements. GitHub hosts code repositories and presentation results. Meetecho streams the kickoff and closing. Webex accounts allow team meetings. HackNet, a Layer 2 VPN, provides remote participants access to IETF network capabilities. The IETF Network Operations Center (NOC) provides wired and wireless access and special networking features (IPv4/IPv6 addressing, closed user groups, NAT64, prefix delegation).
sections.plainLanguage: Teams use the IETF website, email, GitHub, and video conference tools to organize and share their work. The IETF network team helps with internet access and special network features.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
Hackathon Chair(s): organize and deliver each hackathon, encourage and guide project champions, maintain the wiki, moderate email, request sessions, emcee the event, manage the GitHub repository, and serve as the main point of contact. Secretariat: manages registration, maintains the website and wiki, handles venue logistics (room, food, AV), validates registrations for in-person participants, issues badges and T-shirts, and handles IETF-wide promotion.

Sponsors: provide funding and optional T-shirts or giveaways, and optionally offer support staff. They receive logo placement on T-shirts, signage, web pages, and recognition in presentations and the IETF blog. Project Champions: propose projects, manage their teams, encourage collaboration, and produce results presentations. Participation by long-time IETF contributors as champions is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: The Hackathon Chair leads the event. The Secretariat handles logistics. Sponsors help pay. Project leaders (champions) organize their teams. Everyone works together to make it successful.
